To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the out-of-pocket costs for medical care incurred by families of children with incomes less than 200 percent of the poverty line are higher, relative to ability to meet these costs, than for families with higher incomes; and (2) families of children with income below the poverty line, who have no insurance coverage and who do not receive public support, have the highest out-of-pocket costs, relative to their ability to meet these expenses.

(1) the financial burdens incurred in providing medical services for children appear to increase with family income in absolute terms, (2) the financial burdens of medical care for children are distributed regressively when measured in relative terms, and (3) children with continuous Medicaid insurance have substantially lower financial burdens in obtaining medical services than children with no insurance or with intermittent insurance.
(1) the out-of-pocket costs of medical care for children increase with family income and (2) these out-of-pocket costs, relative to the ability to pay, are regressive.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the distribution of the financial burden of medical care for children.
the financial burdens incurred in paying for medical services for children and the distribution of those burdens among families of different incomes.
the distribution of financial burdens associated with obtaining medical care for children, and the extent to which these burdens are distributed equitably.

children in families with higher incomes have greater access to medical care than those in lower-income families.
the financial burden of medical care is not distributed equitably among low income families.
children with continuous Medicaid are much less likely to have high out-of-pocket medical costs than other poor children.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the financial burden of medical care expenses for children is distributed inequitably among families with different income levels.
, in general, children in families with lower income levels are more likely to have a financial burden associated with their health care than children in families with higher income levels.

out-of-pocket costs for children are regressive, but that the poorest children are the least likely to have any out-of-pocket costs at all.
